ask.guide.2: Before we go on: how big do you think the area behind one single value is? The answer is on this page.
ask.guide.3: Observe: in what unit is it measured, and how many years do we have? With only a few years nobody could talk about a trend.
ask.guide.4: Observe: are the last years above or below the first ones?
ask.guide.4.a: The first {k} years average {first}. The last {k} years average {last}.
ask.guide.5: Compare: does the dashed line go where you expected? Do the points stay close to it, or jump far away?
ask.guide.6: Analyze: look at the second bar. Does the range touch zero?
ask.guide.6.clear: It does not touch zero. Every reasonable value points the same way, so the direction is clear.
ask.guide.6.cross: It crosses zero. The change could be up, down or nothing, so the direction is not settled.
ask.guide.7: Evaluate: could you explain to someone what changed, where, how much and with what evidence? Try it before reading on.
ask.guide.8: Evaluate: if you had to check this result yourself, where would you start?
ask.hunch.hidden: By eye it was hard to tell. Using every year at once, the test finds a clear direction.
ask.hunch.lean: The line does lean that way. But the lean is small next to the swings from year to year, so the test cannot confirm it.
ask.hunch.match: That is also what the test finds.
ask.hunch.other: The full record points another way. It happens to everyone: the eye follows a few striking years, the test weighs all of them.

ask.hyp.fb.up: You see the points climbing. Keep one question in mind: is the climb bigger than the usual zigzag from one year to the next?

audit.concl: {real} of the {cats} EONET categories show a real trend. {artifact} are catalog artifacts, {none} shows no trend and {few} have too few events to test.
audit.concl0: None of the {cats} EONET categories shows a real trend. {artifact} are catalog artifacts, {none} shows no trend and {few} have too few events to test.
audit.how.d: A break is a year when the source mix shifts (total variation ≥ 0.5). A four-fold jump in the count is also a break, and so is coverage starting or stopping. The same goes for a Pettitt step that lines up with a catalog-wide break. We keep the longest span with no break (at least {years} years, {mean}+ events a year). We test only that span, with Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen.
audit.lead: EONET lists the natural events that its partner sources report. Sources joined and left over the years. So a rising count can mean a growing catalog, not a changing planet. We audit every category for catalog breaks before we test any trend.
audit.read.artifact: The count changes by {naive} from the first to the last years. But the jumps line up with catalog breaks in {years}. That is the catalog changing, not the planet.
audit.read.artifact.jumps: Coverage starts, stops and jumps at catalog breaks in {years}. The count follows the catalog, not the planet.
audit.read.artifact.nospan: No clean span is long enough to test.
audit.read.artifact.span: In the clean span {from}–{to} there is no trend (p {p}).
audit.read.insufficient: {n} events since {from}: too few to test.
audit.read.no-trend: Over {from}–{to}, with no catalog break, the count holds steady: {rate} a decade, p {p}.
audit.read.trend: In {from}–{to}, a span with no catalog break, events change by {rate} a decade (p {p}).

gloss.break.d: A year when the event list itself changed. Its mix of sources shifted, or its count suddenly rose or fell.
gloss.ci.d: The speeds of change that fit the data. Ranges built this way miss the true speed only rarely.
gloss.merra.d: A NASA model that rebuilds past weather across the whole planet. Measurements from satellites, stations, balloons and aircraft guide it.
gloss.mk.d: Compares each year with every later year, counting rises and falls. Far more of one kind shows a direction.
gloss.ndvi.d: A satellite index of how green and dense vegetation is. On land, it goes from near 0 (bare ground) to about 0.9 (dense forest).
gloss.p.d: The chance of seeing a trend at least this strong if there were no real trend.
gloss.pct.d: The percent of earlier years here that had a lower value than this one. Near either end means unusual.
gloss.reanalysis.d: A NASA model constrained by millions of observations, giving consistent data everywhere, every day since 1980.
gloss.sen.d: The typical speed of change, robust to outliers.
gloss.sig.d: Unlikely to be produced by random variation alone. It does not mean large or important.
gloss.span.d: The longest stretch with no change in how the event list was built. Only those years are tested.
gloss.theilsen.d: The middle value of the change per year, measured between every pair of years. One odd year cannot drag it.
gloss.trend.d: A change that keeps the same direction over many years.
gloss.verdict.d: Confirmed: random year-to-year ups and downs would rarely make a pattern this strong. Inconclusive: it could be chance.
gloss.z.d: How many usual swings this value is above or below the average of earlier years.

method.anom.d: For each natural event in EONET, we take the {days} days before it was first reported. We compare them with the same calendar window in every year since 1981, using NASA POWER daily data. We check daily high, rainfall and soil wetness, and keep the most unusual. A record or a value outside the most extreme 2.5 % on either side counts as anomalous.
method.audit.d: Before counting events, we look for years when the catalog itself changed. Signs of a change: new sources join, volume jumps four-fold, coverage starts or stops. We only test a trend inside the longest stretch with none of those breaks, at least 8 years long.
method.audit.t: Catalog audit: did the list change?
method.gloss.title: Glossary
method.lead: Nature is noisy. A few warm years do not make a warming trend. One record month does not make a disaster. A longer list of events can just mean more people are counting. We use three tests, one for each kind of evidence.
method.limits.d: A point value represents a grid cell of about 50 km (MERRA-2) or a 2 × 2 km box (MODIS). Consecutive years can be correlated, which makes p-values look smaller than they are. A significant trend tells us something changed, not why: the “Why” sections cite the leading scientific explanations.
method.limits.title: Honest limits
method.more.title: Two more tests
method.play.lead: Set a real trend and an amount of noise. Watch when the test can, and cannot, see the trend.
method.play.title: Try it: make your own planet
method.proc.title: How we collect and test the data
method.rare.bar.strong: Anomalous: a record or the 2.5 % tails
method.rare.lead: Looking at more variables makes a false alarm more likely. Pick how many you check and how strict the bar is.
method.rare.result: With no real anomaly, {pct} of 100 random days would still look this extreme. A day counts if at least one of {k} variables looks this way. That is about 1 in {n}.
method.rare.title: Try it: peak or record?
method.s1.d: Summer and winter would look like a trend. We use one value per year: the yearly mean, or the mean of the growing season for vegetation.
method.s2.d: Mann-Kendall compares every year with every later year. If later years are higher far more often than lower, the series has a direction.
method.s3.d: Theil-Sen takes the median of the slopes between all pairs of years. One extreme year cannot drag it.
method.s4.d: We check how often random year-to-year noise would produce this pattern. If it is less than 5 % of the time (p < 0.05), we call the trend significant.
method.title: How to tell a real trend from chance

place.lead: Here the yearly air temperature changes {rate} °C per decade ({from}–{to}). The planet, measured the same way at {points} evenly spread points, changes {global} °C per decade.
place.limits: This file is computed in your browser the moment you open it. One point is a model cell about 50 km wide, so a city and its surroundings share a value. Change the variable above to test rain, soil water, humidity or sunlight with the same method.
place.meta: YOUR PLACE · BUILT LIVE FROM NASA DATA
place.notfound: No place called “{q}”. Try another spelling.
place.sources: NASA POWER monthly and daily (MERRA-2) · NASA GIBS · NASA EONET
pt.air.src: CAMS global model (Copernicus) via Open-Meteo · from Aug 2022
pt.air.story: Daily mean {mean} µg/m³ over {n} days; {above} days above the WHO guideline of {who} µg/m³. Peak {peak} on {date}.
pt.context.d: Other public sources, shown apart from the NASA evidence. They help read the place; they are not part of any verdict.
pt.country.none: This point is not inside a country.
pt.country.src: World Bank indicators · country located with OpenStreetMap Nominatim
pt.fauna.effort.flat: Observation effort is roughly steady over the last {n} years.
pt.fauna.effort.up: Observation effort is growing: more records can mean more observers, not more wildlife.
pt.fauna.none: No records of threatened species within {km} km.
pt.fauna.src: GBIF occurrence records · IUCN Red List categories
pt.fauna.story: {threat} records of IUCN threatened species within {km} km, out of {all} records in total. By category: CR {cr} · EN {en} · VU {vu}.
pt.heat.d: Days a year when the heat index reaches the NOAA “danger” level, 39.4 °C. The heat index uses temperature and humidity at the daily maximum. NASA POWER daily, MERRA-2.
pt.heat.none: No day reached the NOAA danger level since {from}.
pt.heat.story: {first} days in {from}, {last} in {to}. The trend is {rate} days a decade.
pt.orbit.d: MODIS/Terra true color, {date} · NASA GIBS. Clouds can hide the ground; step the day to look again.
pt.recent.d: {start} to {end} against the same 90 days in {n} earlier years ({from}–{to}). NASA POWER daily.
pt.tile.d: NASA EONET events whose point falls inside the hexagon you picked, about {km} km across, {period}.
pt.tile.none: No NASA EONET events fall inside this hexagon {period}.
pt.unreachable: {src} did not respond from this network.
rail.data: NASA data as of {date} · EONET live
ro.ci.clear: 95 % interval from {lo} to {hi}. It stays on one side of zero: the direction is clear.
ro.ci.cross: 95 % interval from {lo} to {hi}. It crosses zero: the direction is not settled.
ro.ci.q: How big, and could it be zero?
ro.lead: The test as three questions, drawn from the exact numbers in the fold below.
ro.p.strong: Strong: p is below 0.01, the stricter of our two lines.
ro.p.weak: Weak: p is above 0.05, so we do not call it a trend.
ro.strip.lead: Each dot is the same {days}-day window in one year since {from}. The large dot is the year of the event.
source.context: Context beyond NASA, labelled apart. It includes CAMS PM2.5 (Copernicus, via Open-Meteo) and GBIF species records. Also World Bank indicators, OpenStreetMap Nominatim and Open-Meteo geocoding.
source.eonet: Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker, NASA Goddard. Curated events from partner sources, 2000–today.
source.gibs: Global Imagery Browse Services, NASA ESDIS. Daily MODIS/Terra true-color imagery since 2000.
source.modis: MOD13Q1 vegetation index from the Terra satellite, 250 m, every 16 days since 2000.
source.power: Reanalysis MERRA-2 served by NASA Langley. Monthly, 0.5° × 0.625°, 1981–2025.
src.d.eonet: The event record: dates, track, sources.
src.d.heat: Daily maximum temperature and humidity, combined into the NOAA heat index.
src.d.modis: 16-day NDVI, 250 m, averaged over the growing season.
src.d.partner: The agency that reported the event to EONET.
src.d.power: Monthly values, averaged per complete year.
src.d.powerDaily: Daily values; the {days}-day window against the same window each year.
src.d.script: Open script that downloads the series and computes the test.
st1.d: NASA's Terra satellite and the MERRA-2 reanalysis record the planet every day.
st1.how: MODIS on Terra sees vegetation at 250 m. MERRA-2 combines millions of observations with a physics model. It gives temperature, rain and soil water everywhere since 1980.
st2.d: Public NASA services, no login: POWER, ORNL DAAC, EONET and GIBS.
st2.how: An open Python script (scripts/build_cases.py) downloads every series and stores it with the case file. Anyone can run it again and get the same numbers.
st3.d: One value per year, so the seasons don't look like a trend.
st3.how: The yearly mean for climate variables. For vegetation, the mean of the growing season: June–September in the Amazon, July–August in the Arctic.
st4.d: Mann-Kendall for the direction, Theil-Sen for the speed, a 95 % band for the uncertainty.
st4.how: Both tools are non-parametric: they don't assume a bell curve, and one extreme year cannot fool them.
st5.d: Strong, moderate or weak evidence, written in plain words.
st5.how: p < 0.01 is strong, p < 0.05 moderate, anything else weak. Weak means “not proven”, never “no change”.
team.ai.d: We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, draft copy and review statistics. Every number comes from NASA data processed by our open scripts, and the team checked each case by hand.
team.lead: Built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.
team.lead2: Earth Trend Detective is a portal that tells real trends from noise with open NASA data. We built it for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”
team.more: More teammates will be added before submission.
team.thanks.d: NASA POWER (Langley Research Center), ORNL DAAC and the MODIS science team. Also NASA EONET (Goddard), NASA GIBS (ESDIS) and NASA Space Apps.
team.thanks.lead: The data and services this portal stands on.
team.title: The team
tl.events.d: Newest first. The figure is how the {days} days before each event compare with the same days in earlier years.
tl.trends.d: Each bar spans the years of measurements behind the trend.
verdict.artifact.d: The apparent change lines up with catalog breaks.
verdict.insufficient.d: Not enough events for a fair test.
verdict.no-trend.d: A clean span exists and the count holds steady.
verdict.trend.d: A significant change inside a span with no catalog break.

w3.tile.none: No NASA EONET events in this tile {period}.
